title: Many a Friend Is a Spear with Crooked Joints
intro: Al-Sharif al-Radi describes a friend whose smile gives no hint of what he harbours. He begins with a spear that resists straightening and ends up considering whether he could bear to part with his own hand. Usama ibn Munqidh included a selection in his anthology Lubab al-adab alongside other poems on difficult friendships. The full poem follows the cost of keeping the friend all the way to the cost of losing him.

translation: Many a friend is a spear with crooked joints
that will not straighten, however long I press it.
1.sharh: A spear shaft has joints that must line up. The time spent pressing it straight stands for the years of trying to bring a friend round.

translation: I accepted the bright face he showed me.
Behind my back he folded away a scowl.
2.sharh: His own part is to accept the welcome he is offered. His friend does something much more deliberate, folding away the feelings that might give him away.

translation: He showed me a meadow on high ground, all tender shoots,
and kept a darkness like the black of night inside.
3.sharh: Fresh growth makes the outward aspect almost inviting to touch. The darkness inside it offers nothing the eye can investigate.

translation: Had I laid his secret heart bare,
I would be holding a wake today for our friendship.
4.sharh: Finding out the whole truth would give him the office of mourner. What dies in that imagined scene is the bond between two people who are still alive.

translation: No hand of mine goes out to hurt him if he hurts me,
no mouth opens to revile him if he gives me cause.
5.sharh: The two restraints have different occasions, an actual injury and grounds for suspicion. Hand and open mouth make visible the replies he withholds.

translation: He is a limb on which the nights have laid an affliction.
Whoever carries an aching limb must feel its pain.
6.sharh: The crooked spear could at least be laid aside. With a limb the person who chooses to keep it must carry its pain in his own body.

translation: When the wise physician orders it cut off,
I treasure it and say, “Perhaps”, and “Maybe yet”.
7.sharh: The physician can make a definite recommendation. The patient cannot finish either of his hopeful phrases, but their hesitation is enough to put off the operation.

translation: I endure its pain for fear of the loss.
Whoever blames someone past heeding deserves more blame.
8.sharh: An ache can still be borne tomorrow. A missing limb cannot be restored. The recurring sound of “blame” turns the charge back on the person who keeps reproaching.

translation: It is my hand. To keep it diseased is agony.
Cut off, it disfigures the forearm and the wrist.
9.sharh: Only now do we see which limb he has in mind. Removing the source of pain would alter the shape even of the sound arm attached to it.

translation: Though you defy me, I hold you dearer
than my own obedient heart, and in higher honour.
10.sharh: He finally turns to “you”. The heart that does the valuing is itself put in the balance against its troublesome friend and comes off second best.

translation: I bear you as an eye bears a stubborn speck,
never clearing for a day, never quite going blind.
11.sharh: A speck can command all one's attention without destroying sight. That middle condition, short of cure and short of blindness, is what makes endurance possible.

translation: Leave a man folded round the fault you found in him.
Do not lay the deep-seated illness open and regret it.
12.sharh: The friend can be left folded like a cloth. To spread the fault for inspection also spreads the illness, a danger that disclosure itself brings about.

translation: Cut off each limb the moment it hurts you,
however ruefully, and you will leave no flesh or blood.
13.sharh: Even a reluctant amputation is final. Applied to every fresh hurt, a rule meant to preserve the body would gradually do away with it.

translation: Whoever fails to brace himself for a little hurt
lays himself open to meeting something graver and greater.
14.sharh: The ending asks what a person can train himself to bear. Losing someone altogether may turn out to be the greater injury a quick remedy invites.

1.1.4.head: زاغَ
1.1.4.meaning: Swerved or fell out of line, here at the joints of the shaft.

1.1.5.head: كَعب
1.1.5.meaning: A raised joint in the cane from which a spear shaft is made.

1.2.4.head: غَمز
1.2.4.meaning: Pressure applied by hand to straighten something bent.

2.2.1.head: أَدمَجَ
2.2.1.meaning: Folded up and concealed, here his ill will.

3.1.3.head: الحَزن
3.1.3.meaning: Rough upland. The diwan also identifies al-Hazn as a tract of meadows and hollows belonging to Banu Yarbu'.

3.2.3.head: الخُدارِيّ
3.2.3.meaning: Intensely black, here of impenetrable night.

4.1.5.head: ضَمير
4.1.5.meaning: A person's private thoughts and feelings.

4.2.6.head: مَأتَم
4.2.6.meaning: A gathering for mourning, held here for a friendship.

5.2.2.head: فاغِر
5.2.2.meaning: With mouth open wide, ready to speak ill of someone.

6.1.4.meaning: The passing nights, representing the blows that time can deal.

7.1.3.head: الطِّبّ
7.1.3.meaning: A skilled physician, the person whose judgement the patient evades.

7.2.3.head: ضَنّ
7.2.3.meaning: Reluctance to part with something dearly held.

7.2.5.head: لَعَلَّما
7.2.5.meaning: “And perhaps.” The hoped-for recovery never has to be said aloud.

8.2.5.head: اِرعَوى
8.2.5.meaning: To desist or take a rebuke to heart.

9.1.3.head: مَضّ
9.1.3.meaning: Acute, wearing pain, here the cost of keeping the hand.

9.2.5.head: مِعصَم
9.2.5.meaning: The wrist, where a bracelet encircles the arm.

10.1.6.head: عاصٍ
10.1.6.meaning: Defiant or ungovernable, set against his own obedient heart.

11.1.4.meaning: Persisted, here of a speck that will not shift.

11.1.6.head: قَذى
11.1.6.meaning: A speck of dust or chaff caught in the eye.

12.1.3.head: مَطوِيّ
12.1.3.meaning: Folded up, with what lies inside left private.

12.2.4.head: عُضال
12.2.4.meaning: Intractable, of a disease or a deeply rooted fault.

13.2.1-2.head: عَلى مَضَض
13.2.1-2.meaning: “In pain.” The decision to amputate is taken with real distress.

14.1.3.head: وَطَّنَ
14.1.3.meaning: To school oneself to endure something. The object “oneself” is implicit.

14.2.4.head: أَجَلّ
14.2.4.meaning: Graver in consequence, here of an injury.
